rationale: Start with a broad, mid-temperature scouting gradient that is very unlikely to miss late-eluting compounds and should spread the full mixture across the run. This first run maps the overall elution window and reveals whether the main need is narrower composition bounds, a different slope, or a temperature shift.

All 10 compounds eluted well within the gradient, so the next step is to trim the composition window to the actual elution region to reduce the time penalty while keeping similar selectivity. A 0.10–0.60 window should still cover the observed phi_e range and test whether we can keep full resolution with a shorter effective retention span.

The broad window at 20 min already gave perfect resolution, so the best opportunity is to cut analysis time by steepening the same successful gradient. This directly measures how much the critical mid-run pairs, especially 6/7, depend on slope while likely improving CRF if resolution stays acceptable.

The 10 min gradient is fast but over-compresses the critical 5–7 cluster, while 20 min fully resolves it, so the optimum should lie between them. A 14 min run directly tests that tradeoff and may recover enough resolution on the 6/7 pair while keeping the time penalty near zero.

The critical 6/7 pair improves strongly with shallower slope, and 14 min is already close to optimal, so a small move to 16 min is the most direct way to test whether we can push that pair closer to full resolution while still keeping zero time penalty. This is a local refinement around the current best method.

The 6/7 pair is the only remaining weak spot and may need a selectivity change more than further slope adjustment, so test a modest temperature shift while keeping the near-optimal 14 min gradient. A 5 C decrease is enough to probe whether temperature can open that close pair without sacrificing the fast run.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity by shifting the problem from 6/7 to 5/6, so the complementary test is a 5 C increase at the same near-optimal slope. This will show whether the critical cluster opens in the opposite thermal direction and could surpass the current best.

Temperature changes both worsened the critical cluster, so the best direction remains slope-only optimization around 40 C. Since 16 min already fully resolves all pairs but pays a small time penalty, 18 min checks whether the CRF surface is peaking sharply there or whether 16 min was already beyond the optimum.

The active elution window is much narrower than 0.05–0.95, and all peaks elute by about phi_e ~0.45, so lowering phi1 slightly may preserve the favorable selectivity around the crowded cluster while trimming the late high-organic segment. This probes whether a modestly narrower window can improve CRF without the strong retention penalty seen for 0.10–0.60.

Narrowing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved CRF, so the next logical refinement is another small step down to see if the crowded mid-run cluster gains a bit more from a tighter window without incurring the large retention penalty seen for much lower phi1. This is a local optimization around the current best method.

At phi1 0.90 the run still has zero time penalty, so a slightly steeper gradient may shorten the method further while keeping the now-improved selectivity from the narrower window. This tests whether the current best is on the flat top of the time term or whether a small reduction in tG can reach an even higher CRF.

The 12 min run compressed the critical 6/7 pair too much, while 14 min at phi1 0.90 is the current best, so the next useful local test is a slightly shallower 16 min gradient with the same narrowed window. This checks whether the gain in 6/7 resolution can outweigh any small time penalty and possibly surpass the current optimum.

At 14 min and phi1 0.90 the method is already near-optimal, so a stronger temperature perturbation than ±5 C is worthwhile to probe whether the close 6/7 pair has a non-monotonic selectivity response that was missed. A 30 C run keeps the best slope/window constant while giving a more decisive thermal selectivity test.

Lower temperatures clearly degrade selectivity across the crowded cluster, so the remaining unexplored thermal direction is a stronger increase above 45 C. Running 50 C at the current best window and slope tests whether higher temperature may improve the key pair after the poor result at 45 C or confirms that 40 C is the selectivity optimum.

The optimum appears centered near 40 C and 14 min, and narrowing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved CRF while 0.85 remained strong, so one more small step to phi1 0.80 is worth testing. This probes whether a tighter gradient window can further improve the critical 6/7 spacing enough to offset any modest increase in retention time.

We have established that 40 C is best among the temperatures tried, but with 10 injections left it is still worth closing the temperature space by testing the lower bound once at the current best gradient. This confirms whether the thermal selectivity trend is monotonic and rules out an unexpected optimum at the edge before focusing the remaining runs on composition-window refinement.

The remaining opportunity is fine tuning the gradient window around the current best method, and raising phi0 slightly may reduce early dead space while subtly changing selectivity in the crowded middle without the strong penalty seen when the whole window was shifted too low. This is a focused test of whether the optimal window starts a bit higher than 0.05 while keeping the successful phi1 and slope.

Raising phi0 to 0.10 improved the best method, so the next local refinement is to pair that higher start with the slightly lower phi1 that also performed well. This tests whether a tighter 0.10–0.85 window can preserve full coverage while nudging the critical 6/7 pair and run time to an even better CRF.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so the remaining runs can only map the optimum plateau and identify a robust backup nearby. Lowering phi1 one more step from the winning method tests how sharply performance falls on the tighter-window side while keeping all other successful settings fixed.

With the maximum CRF already achieved at 0.10–0.85, the best use of the remaining budget is to define the robustness of that optimum. Increasing phi0 one more step tests whether the plateau extends toward a slightly stronger starting composition, which could further reduce early idle time while preserving the excellent mid-run selectivity.

Two adjacent windows, 0.10–0.85 and 0.15–0.85, both achieve the maximum CRF, so the next informative move is to continue stepping phi0 upward to locate the edge of the optimum plateau. This tests whether a still stronger starting composition remains fully effective or begins to erode early retention/selectivity.

The optimum plateau now appears to lie near phi0 0.10–0.15 and phi1 0.85, so the most useful remaining test is the adjacent upper-right corner, 0.15–0.90. This checks whether the maximum also extends to a slightly wider upper bound or whether phi1 0.85 is the true optimum along that axis.

With the best CRF already at 1.000, the remaining value is to map nearby robustness in slope around a winning window. Testing the steeper 12 min version of the 0.10–0.85 optimum shows how much margin there is before the critical 6/7 pair begins to compress.

Since both 0.10–0.85 and 0.15–0.85 give the maximum at 14 min, testing the steeper 12 min gradient at the other winning window maps robustness on slope across the plateau. This tells whether the slightly higher phi0 tolerates compression better and identifies the stronger backup method.

The last run should complete the local map around the two winning methods by testing the lower-phi1 corner adjacent to 0.15–0.85. This confirms whether phi1 = 0.85 is the true optimum at phi0 = 0.15 or if the maximum plateau extends downward as well.
